title: The poem, its date and text
short: Written about 1861-62 (Franklin 340, Johnson 280) and first printed in 1896 without its final stanza; the archive gives the 1896 text.
body: The manuscript is in Fascicle 16; Johnson dates it 1861 and Franklin about 1862. Mabel Loomis Todd printed it in Poems: Third Series (1896), regularising punctuation (the manuscript's dashes become commas), lowering capitals ('Funeral', 'Brain', 'Being') and omitting the fifth stanza, which describes 'a Plank in Reason' breaking and the speaker falling through 'World' after 'World'. That stanza was first printed in 1947 and is now restored in modern editions. The archive's text therefore ends with 'Wrecked, solitary, here', a different conclusion from Dickinson's: an image of isolation rather than of a fall into unconsciousness.

title: The funeral as inner event
short: The poem follows a New England funeral step by step (mourners, service, carrying the coffin, tolling bell) as a figure for a mental crisis.
body: Nineteenth-century Amherst funerals were domestic: mourners gathered at the house, a service was held, the coffin was carried out and the church bell tolled. Dickinson, who lived in the centre of Amherst and attended many funerals, knew the sequence well. Transferring it 'in my Brain' makes the speaker both the corpse and the witness. Critics read the crisis variously: as madness or nervous breakdown, as severe depression, as a loss of faith, or as an account of losing consciousness; the poem's precision about sensations and vagueness about cause allow all these.

title: treading, treading
short: The repeated participle imitates the monotonous tread of feet, pressing on the mind until it gives way.
body: Repetition ('treading, treading'; 'beating, beating') is the poem's main sound device. It imitates the heavy, rhythmic sounds of the funeral and the pounding of a headache, and it slows the hymn metre into something oppressive. Each stanza has a similar shape: a ritual action, a repeated verb, and a consequence for the mind ('till it seemed', 'till I thought'). The present participles also suspend time, so that the ritual seems endless, and the relentless pattern prepares for the moment when the repetition stops and space itself begins to toll.

title: sense was breaking through
short: A crux: is reason breaking down, or is some new awareness breaking through into the mind?
body: 'Sense' can mean reason, the faculty of understanding, or the bodily senses and perception. 'Breaking through' can mean collapsing (like a floor giving way, anticipating the 'Plank in Reason' of the omitted stanza) or emerging (like light breaking through). Some readers take the line to say that the treading is about to break the mind; others that a painful clarity or awareness is forcing its way in. Dickinson's dictionary (Webster) lists both 'understanding' and 'perception by the senses' among the meanings of 'sense'. The ambiguity is generally considered deliberate.

title: A service like a drum
short: The funeral service is heard only as a drumbeat, a meaningless rhythm, as if words had become pure sound.
body: The service, which should offer words of consolation, becomes a percussive noise. The drum also recalls military funerals, where muffled drums beat time for the procession, and the pulse of blood in the head. That its effect is numbness ('My mind was going numb') suggests that ritual, far from consoling, overwhelms the speaker. This is one ground for reading the poem as sceptical of religious consolation.

title: numb
short: Numbness is the poem's first stage of loss: thought dulls before it collapses entirely.
body: Dickinson writes often about numbness as the mind's response to great pain, most famously in 'After great pain, a formal feeling comes' (Franklin 372), with its 'Hour of Lead'. Here the mind goes numb under the drumbeat; in the next stanza the boots are 'of lead', another link between the two poems. The sequence (treading, numbness, loss of space and selfhood) charts an unusually precise phenomenology of collapse.

title: a box
short: The coffin, named with deliberate plainness as "a box", is lifted and carried across the soul.
body: Calling the coffin 'a box' is typical of Dickinson's defamiliarising understatement. The speaker hears rather than sees: the poem is entirely auditory, as if experienced from inside the coffin with eyes closed. The pallbearers 'creak across my soul', the soul becoming a floor of creaking boards: the mind is now a house, with a floor that may give way, which is exactly what happens in the manuscript's final stanza, where 'a Plank in Reason' breaks.

title: boots of lead
short: Heavy, leaden footsteps: lead suggests weight, dullness, and the lead lining of coffins.
body: Lead is proverbially heavy and dull, and in Dickinson's poems it often figures paralysing grief ('the Hour of Lead'). 'Those same boots' refers back to the treading mourners of stanza 1; the funeral has come full circle. 'Again' marks the oppressive repetition. Early coffins were sometimes lead-lined, which adds a further, literal association. The heaviness of the boots presses on the 'soul' as the treading of stanza 1 pressed on the brain, keeping the poem's movement inward and downward.

title: space began to toll
short: The funeral bell is heard as if the whole of space were ringing, a synaesthetic expansion of sound to the cosmos.
body: At a funeral the church bell tolls (rings slowly, with pauses). Dickinson makes space itself the bell: sound fills the universe. The sentence runs on across the stanza break ('toll / As all the heavens'), the only place where it does so, enacting the sudden enlargement. The following lines ('As all the heavens were a bell, / And Being but an ear') extend the conceit: the cosmos rings and existence is reduced to hearing.

title: Being but an ear
short: All existence, or the speaker's own being, is reduced to a single organ of hearing, passive and overwhelmed.
body: 'As all the heavens were a bell' is a subjunctive ('as if all the heavens were'). 'Being' (capitalised even in the 1896 text) may mean existence in general or the speaker's own self. If the heavens are a bell and Being only an ear, there is no room left for thought or will: the self is pure, passive reception. Some readers see this as a mystical moment, others as the final stage of mental breakdown; the omitted last stanza, where the speaker falls and 'Finished knowing', supports the second.

title: I and silence some strange race
short: 'Race' most likely means kind or species: the speaker and silence form a strange new breed, set apart from humanity.
body: 'Race' in Webster includes 'the descendants of a common ancestor; a family, tribe, people', and also a running contest. The first sense is generally preferred: 'I' and 'silence' are the last two members of some strange species, cast away together. The personification of silence as a companion is striking: after the noise of treading, drumming and tolling, silence is all that remains. The manuscript reads 'And I, and Silence, some strange Race'.

title: Wrecked, solitary, here
short: The shipwreck image ends the 1896 text in isolation; Dickinson's own fifth stanza instead continues to a fall through worlds.
body: The speaker and silence are like castaways after a shipwreck, alone 'here' (an unspecified place). In the 1896 printing these are the last words, leaving the poem in stunned stasis. In Dickinson's manuscript the poem goes on: a 'Plank in Reason' breaks, and the speaker drops down and down, hitting a world at every plunge, and 'Finished knowing - then -'. Critics note that the restored ending changes the poem's shape from burial to fall, and ends on an unfinished dash: whether this means unconsciousness, madness, death or a new kind of knowledge is left unresolved.

title: Hymn metre and slant rhyme
short: Five (here four) quatrains in common metre rhyming on lines 2 and 4 with one slant pair, a hymn form turned against consolation.
body: Like most of Dickinson's poems, this one uses the hymn stanza (alternating four- and three-stress lines). The rhymes on lines 2 and 4 are full ('soul/toll', 'drum/numb', 'ear/here') except the slant 'fro/through'. The familiar church metre is ironically apt for a funeral, but the poem offers none of the consolation the hymns promised. The 1896 editors replaced Dickinson's dashes with commas and periods, smoothing a rhythm that in the manuscript is broken and halting.
